chapter: Chicago cafes and the Browns band
title: Hearing the Browns band from New Orleans at Lamb's Cafe, 1915
summary: Frisco raved about the Browns band until Corbett hired them; Jernberg heard only the trio playing dinner music in July 1915 and never heard the whole band.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, I tell you, he heard this Browns band from Dixieland in New Orleans, and he come back to Chicago to Smiley Corbett's Cafe there, the Lamb's Cafe, raving about this Browns band from Dixieland. And he kept on raving and kept on raving until Smiley Corbett finally gave up and had the band come up. And Corbett was still of the old school, pretty much. He thought they ought to be playing dinner music at night, you know. Boy, what a joke that is. Yeah. So, the full band didn't play the dinner music. The red brown switch from trombone to guitar, and there was a string bass, and Gus Miller playing clarinet. Yeah. And I went down to hear them play. I heard so much about a jazz band, and I had never heard a jazz band in my life and didn't know what jazz sounded like. And this was the summer of 1915, about July around there. I went down there one night to have dinner before going out to the Sheridan Inn at Broadway and Devon where I worked at night. And here were these three guys, and I thought, well, gee whiz, this is not so hot. Where's the rest of the band, huh? And you know what they started to play for dinner music? This guitar, string bass, and clarinet, black and white rag, strictly Dixieland style. Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.
And, boy, was that comical. And I never did get to hear that whole band either, because that was the only time of the night I could get down there. They weren't in Chicago very long.
They left and went to New York for a week or two.
